opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the ideas in cooperative AI that I find interesting and a bit underappreciated. A lot of the hope people have is that AIs will be better at cooperation than we are: they'll be more rational, they can process more information, maybe they can even share their source code and verify each other's intentions. Some of that may well turn out to be true. But there's a countervailing consideration worth taking seriously.

Think about why humans manage to bargain as well as we do. We're all running on roughly the same hardware. We share an evolutionary history, a common psychology, and a lot of common culture. When I'm negotiating with you, I have a pretty good model of what you want, what you fear, what you'd regard as fair, and how you'd react if I pushed too hard. I can simulate you by asking, "What would I do in your shoes?" And that works surprisingly well, because your shoes and my shoes are similar. We also share focal points, like splitting the difference or "first come, first served," that let us coordinate without spelling everything out.

Now imagine AI systems that were trained by different labs, on different data, with different architectures and objectives, possibly deployed by different states or companies with very different goals. There's no guarantee they share that common ground. Their internal representations might be quite alien to each other. Their notions of what's fair or what's a reasonable concession could differ, and they may not have shared focal points. And the "put myself in your shoes" trick doesn't work as well when the other party's shoes are a completely different shape.

Bargaining theory tells us that a lot of costly conflict comes from uncertainty and from incompatible beliefs about the other side: about their resolve, their capabilities, or what they'll accept. If AIs are more opaque to one another than humans are to each other, that uncertainty could be larger, not smaller. You could get more miscalculation, more brinkmanship that goes wrong, and more failures to find the deal that both sides would have preferred to fighting.

There's also a speed and scale dimension. Humans have built up, over centuries, institutions, norms, diplomatic protocols, and reputational mechanisms that help us manage misunderstanding. AI agents interacting at machine speed may not have time to develop those, or the ones we've built may not transfer.

So the upshot isn't that AI cooperation is doomed. It's that we shouldn't assume intelligence automatically yields mutual understanding. Being smart is different from being legible to others. That's a reason to invest deliberately in things like shared protocols, interpretability, ways for agents to credibly communicate their intentions and commitments, and common standards, so we're building the conditions for mutual understanding rather than hoping it emerges on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems may have very different objectives and alien representations, making them harder for one another to understand in bargaining.

r002.rationale: It does not mention linear utility in wealth or contrast it with humans’ diminishing returns.

r003.rationale: It mentions the possibility of sharing source code, but does not question whether an AI would grant its counterpart access to its internal workings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a bit counterintuitive, because the first intuition most people have is the opposite — that AIs should find bargaining easier. They can exchange code, they can run millions of simulations, they don't have egos, and so on. And some of that may well be true. But I think there are a few reasons to worry that in certain respects they could actually be worse off than humans.

The first is that humans share an enormous amount of common ground that we mostly don't notice. We have the same basic cognitive architecture, roughly the same emotions, very similar bodies and needs. When I'm negotiating with another person, I can run a pretty good simulation of them in my own head, because they're built like me. I know what it feels like to be insulted, or to be worried about looking weak, or to want to get home for dinner. That shared architecture gives us a kind of free mutual legibility. Two AI systems trained by different labs, on different data, with different architectures and different objectives, may not have anything like that. Each one might be, from the other's perspective, genuinely alien.

The second thing is that humans have had tens of thousands of years of cultural evolution building up institutions and conventions for bargaining: norms about what counts as a credible threat, what a handshake means, rituals for de-escalating, focal points like "split it down the middle." These are enormously important for getting to agreements, and they're not derived from first principles — they're inherited. AIs won't necessarily share any of that unless we deliberately build it in, and if different systems come with different inherited conventions, they could easily misread each other's signals.

And then the third issue, which I think is maybe the most worrying, is around credibility and commitment. A lot of bargaining is about convincing the other side that you'll actually follow through — that your red line is real. Humans do this imperfectly, but we have a lot of cues: body language, reputation, the costliness of certain signals. With AI systems, you have agents that could in principle be extremely good at deception, or extremely good at verifying each other, and we don't know which regime we'll end up in. If an AI can't tell whether the other system's stated commitment is sincere, or whether it's a strategically generated bluff, then you lose the information that normally lets you find the zone of agreement. And unlike humans, AIs might also be running strategies that are just very hard to interpret — the reasoning behind a demand might be opaque even to the system's own developers, let alone to the counterparty.

So I don't want to say AIs will definitely be worse at this. There are also really exciting possibilities — things like systems being able to verifiably reveal their source code, or make commitments that are enforced by their architecture, which humans simply can't do. But I think the default assumption that intelligence automatically brings mutual understanding is wrong. Understanding another agent is about shared structure and shared history as much as raw capability, and that's exactly what we can't take for granted with AI.

astra-6.text:
Well, humans share a lot of common structure. We have similar brains, we’ve grown up in somewhat similar environments, and we have emotions that give us clues about what someone else wants and how they’ll react. So even when someone is quite different from you, you can use yourself as a rough model of them.

With AIs, that might be much less reliable. They could have very different architectures, training histories, and objectives. One system might find it difficult to infer what another system values, what it believes, or what would convince it to accept a deal. And those are precisely the things you need to understand in bargaining. Is this a credible threat? Is the other side actually willing to walk away, or is it bluffing?

There’s a possible countervailing effect: AIs might be able to share or inspect aspects of their code, or provide guarantees that humans can’t. So it’s not inevitable that they’ll have more difficulty. But greater intelligence alone doesn’t mean that they’ll understand one another, especially if they’re very different kinds of minds.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, humans share a lot of structure. We have similar brains, we’ve grown up in somewhat similar environments, and we have emotions and motivations that we can recognise in one another. That gives us a basis for inferring what someone wants, what they believe, and whether a threat or a promise is credible. We still get those things wrong, but we have a starting point.

With AIs, you could have agents with very different architectures, training histories, and objectives. An agent might be extremely capable at solving problems without having a good model of this particular other agent. And in bargaining, that matters: you want to know what the other side would accept, how it will respond if you refuse, and whether it will actually follow through on a commitment.

There’s a potential advantage in the other direction, which is that AIs might be able to share or inspect code, or provide stronger evidence about what they’ll do than humans can. But access to code doesn’t automatically make the behaviour of a complex system understandable. So I wouldn’t say AIs necessarily will find bargaining harder. The point is that we shouldn’t assume that greater intelligence by itself gives them the shared understanding that makes bargaining work.
